mentions.name: Audion
mentions.description: Audion is a code-first language for creating installations and interactive art. It provides BPM-synchronized threads while also supporting drawing, file IO, networking, and hardware control, combining music timing with general-purpose programming capabilities.
mentions.problem: Existing creative-coding tools fall short: Max/MSP gets messy on very large projects, Python does not work well for music making, and Tidal/Pi/Supercollider are limited to sound only.
mentions.source_excerpt: I needed a code-first approach for making installations and interactive art. MaxMsp gets messy with very big projects. Python didn't really work well for music making and Tidal/Pi/Sclang are only meant for sound. So I needed something that has bpm synchronized threads, but can draw and do anything else like file IO, networking, hardware control etc. It works quite well now.

mentions.name: Audion
mentions.description: Audion is an interpreted scripting language designed to be fun to write, aimed at creating interactive music and audio/visual installations. It integrates with SuperCollider, any DAW, and hardware, and includes built-in BPM synchronization between real OS threads and Ableton sync.
mentions.source_excerpt: Audion, interpreted scripting language that is fun to write and lets you make interactive music, a/v installations using supercollider or any daw and hardware. BPM synchronization between real OS threads and Ableton sync is built in as well.

mentions.name: audion
mentions.description: A programming language for creating and hacking music, with an object system supporting object composition and combinatorics-based functions for generating rhythms and melodies. SuperCollider is tightly integrated but not required, and output can drive hardware, DAWs, or SuperCollider. A nightly release is available, with the full language spec in the docs folder and userland libraries still in development.
mentions.problem: After completing a permanent museum installation using Max/MSP and Python, the author felt musical ideas could be expressed far more easily in a few lines of code, which motivated the language.
